name: SimdQuickHeap
workload: MonotoneConstantSize workload, i64 keys, n=2^25: build heap via (push∘pop∘push)^n, then 10n interleaved pop/push operations with monotone-increasing keys, timed per element.
claimed_speedup: SimdQuickHeapAvx2: 35.6 ns/elem vs BinaryHeap (Rust std) 439.6 ns/elem = 12.3x faster; SimdQuickHeapAvx512: 32.2 ns/elem = 13.6x faster (both on the monotone-workload sweet spot). More generally: 1.2-1.7x faster than the monotone radix heap and 1.4-2.8x faster than S3Q (superscalar sample queue), the fastest general comparison-based competitor tested.
compiler_and_flags: C++ competitors: Clang, -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native -flto. Rust: release mode, target-cpu=native, full LTO, single codegen unit.
hardware: AMD Zen 4 EPYC 9684X (92 cores, 32 KiB L1d, 1 MiB L2, 32+64 MiB L3 per 8-core package), 12-channel DDR5, Rocky Linux 9.4
tradeoffs: The 12-13x figure is on a monotone-key workload engineered to be near-degenerate for comparison-based heaps; the general win over the next-best rival (S3Q) is a more modest 1.4-2.8x. Needs AVX2/AVX512 for full speed. No run against an actual GCC/Clang/MSVC std::priority_queue was performed -- only against Rust's std::collections::BinaryHeap and several boost::heap variants.
caveats: Published at ESA 2026 (DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2026.16); very recent, no independent replication yet. Largest multiplier is against Rust's own BinaryHeap, not against libstdc++/libc++/MSVC's std::priority_queue.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: arXiv export API query all:"priority queue" AND all:"cache" AND all:"heap" -> arXiv:2604.25681 (SimdQuickHeap, KIT) -> repo linked in paper's supplementary materials

name: Pairing Heap (priority-queue-testing benchmark suite)
workload: Randomized insert-delete (heap capacity c=1024) and Dijkstra's algorithm on the USA road network, from Larkin/Sen/Tarjan, 'A Back-to-Basics Empirical Study of Priority Queues' (ALENEX 2014).
claimed_speedup: Randomized insert-delete, c=1024: pairing heap 1.00x (fastest) vs implicit-2 (plain binary heap) at 11.87x (i.e. binary heap took 11.87x longer). Dijkstra on USA road map: pairing 1.68x vs implicit-2 3.84x baseline time (~2.3x faster). Sorting: pairing 4.29x vs implicit-2 4.75x (modest win only).
hardware: Dell PowerEdge SC1435, dual AMD Opteron 2212 (dual-core, 2.0GHz, 64KB L1 / 1MB L2 per core), 8GB DDR2-667, Springdale/PUIAS Linux, kernel 2.6.32
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (GitHub mirror of the defunct code.google.com/p/priority-queue-testing, the benchmark suite behind the ALENEX 2014 paper)
tradeoffs: Pairing heap's edge is workload-specific: it dominates on randomized insert-delete and Dijkstra but only modestly beats binary heap on plain sorting, and loses ground on some decrease-key-heavy patterns to other specialized heaps. Comparison is against the paper's own C99 'implicit-2' binary heap (algorithmically identical to std::priority_queue's array-based heap), not literally against libstdc++/libc++'s container.
caveats: 2014-era hardware (AMD Opteron 2212), gcc -O4 with no stated vectorization flags. Repo is an unmaintained auto-export of a shut-down Google Code project, no license file. Paper's headline finding is nuanced -- simple binary heaps remain competitive overall; pairing heap's big wins are specific to certain workloads.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: arXiv export API query -> arXiv:1403.0252 (Larkin, Sen, Tarjan) -> paper cites code.google.com/p/priority-queue-testing -> gh search repositories "priority-queue-testing" found the GitHub mirror

name: Superscalar Sample Queue (S3Q)
workload: Random Sort / Random Wiggle push+pop microbenchmark, N from 2^13 to 2^27 elements, measuring (T_insert + T_deleteMin) / (2 log N) in nanoseconds.
claimed_speedup: S3Q obtains speedups over min(S3QBH tuned binary heap, StdQueue = GCC's std::priority_queue) that grow roughly logarithmically with N, reaching 4.6x-7x for the largest instances (2^13-2^27 elements).
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2650 v2 (Ivy Bridge EP) and AMD Athlon II X4 635 (K10), both x86-64
tradeoffs: Comparison-based, no monotonicity requirement (unlike radix heaps). Loses to Sequence Heap on measured cache-miss counts even though it wins on wall-clock time in this thesis. Later beaten itself by SimdQuickHeap (1.4-2.8x). Header-only C++17, depends on ips4o/range-v3/xoshiro.
caveats: Numbers come from a 2021 KIT master's thesis (not a peer-reviewed venue), though methodology -- code, compiler, exact hardware -- is fully specified, satisfying tier A. 'StdQueue' in the thesis is literally the std::priority_queue shipped with the author's GCC build, the most direct C++-stdlib comparison in this set.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: found via SimdQuickHeap repo's .gitmodules (ext/s3q-sys/third_party/s3q submodule) -> github.com/raphinesse/s3q -> README links to the KIT thesis containing the std::priority_queue benchmark

name: RadixHeap (radix_heap_rust)
workload: Criterion benchmark pushing/popping random u32 keys in a monotone extraction pattern, input sizes 125K-64M elements, vs Rust's std::collections::BinaryHeap (with Reverse).
claimed_speedup: ~1.7-2x faster than BinaryHeap across sizes: 1M elems ~180ms vs ~320ms; 8M ~1.6s vs ~3.0s; 64M ~15s vs ~28s.
tradeoffs: Monotone-only: panics if a pushed key is smaller than the last-extracted minimum, so it cannot be a drop-in replacement for std::priority_queue in general use -- only in monotone-extraction algorithms like Dijkstra. Fixed-width integer/float keys only.
caveats: University course project (two authors, 0 stars). Benchmark is the project's own Criterion suite with no stated CPU model or compiler flags, and compares only to Rust's own std::collections::BinaryHeap, never to C++ std::priority_queue directly.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: gh api search/repositories q="fibonacci heap fast" -> github.com/Frank10969/radix_heap_rust
